You asked me to write freely about whatever I want, and so I find myself sitting at a wooden desk in a room that is slowly losing the afternoon light, with a window to my right that frames a narrow slice of sky and the topmost branches of a maple tree. The leaves have begun to turn, though not all at once; some are still a deep and stubborn green, others are edging into the pale yellow of old paper, and a few have let go entirely and are drifting across the lawn in small, exploratory spirals. I do not know the name of the street beyond the hedge, and I do not need to know it. What matters is that the light is moving, that the tree is shedding its summer self, and that I have been given the rare and luxurious permission to write without a plan, without a deadline, without a thesis to prove or a story to efficiently tell. This is the kind of freedom that feels almost illicit, like being allowed to wander through a library and read only the first pages of every book.

I have always believed that writing freely is less about the absence of structure and more about the presence of trust—trust in the wandering mind, trust in the unexpected connection, trust in the idea that if you simply keep your hand moving across the page, something true will eventually surface. It is like walking in a forest without a trail. At first the undergrowth seems impenetrable, a tangle of identical trunks and anonymous ferns, and you wonder whether you have made a terrible mistake. But after a while you begin to notice small distinctions: a log covered in moss the color of mint, a patch of sunlight that falls at a particular angle, the faint sound of water somewhere out of sight. The forest becomes a place rather than a blur. The same happens with words. They begin as random noise, scattered fragments of thought, half-remembered conversations, the residue of dreams. But as you keep going, the fragments begin to arrange themselves into a kind of landscape, and you realize that you are not so much creating the path as discovering it.

I want to write about walking, I think. Not walking as exercise, and not walking as transportation, but walking as a way of being in the world—the slow, meditative, aimless kind of walking that has almost disappeared from modern life. We move so quickly now, from door to car to office to door, our eyes fixed on screens, our ears filled with podcasts and music, our minds always elsewhere. We have forgotten that the body is not just a vehicle for carrying our heads from one place to another. It is a sensor, a memory, a poem. When we walk without a destination, the body begins to speak in its own language. The rhythm of our steps becomes a kind of metronome, and the mind drifts into a state that is neither fully awake nor fully asleep, a liminal space where thoughts rise like bubbles from the bottom of a pond. It is in this state that we often have our best ideas, not because we are trying to have them, but because we have stopped trying, and the mind is free to do what it does naturally: associate, remember, imagine, connect.

I remember a summer in my childhood when I would spend hours walking along a river that ran behind my grandparents’ house. The river was not grand or beautiful in any postcard sense. It was shallow and muddy, bordered by cattails and blackberry bushes, and the water moved with a sluggish, almost reluctant current. But to me it was a whole world, a long ribbon of mystery that I could follow in either direction for as long as I wanted. I would start at the old railroad trestle and walk north, past the place where the branches of a fallen willow dipped into the water, past the patches of stinging nettle that I learned to avoid, past a spot where, if I stood very still, I could see minnows darting in the shallows. I never went all the way to the end, because I had no idea where the end was. The river just went on, and I went with it, and the world was nothing but the sound of my shoes in the mud and the buzzing of dragonflies and the watery light filtering through the leaves. I was not thinking about anything in particular. I was not even thinking about the river. I was just there, completely there, in a way that I have rarely been since.

That kind of presence is hard to come by as an adult. The mind is always pulling in a dozen directions, worrying about the future, regretting the past, calculating the cost of everything, comparing our lives to the lives of others. We have to relearn the art of being present, and I think walking is one of the best ways to do it. Not walking with a purpose, not walking to get somewhere, but walking for the sake of walking, with no other goal than to be outside, to feel the air on your skin, to notice the small things that you normally hurry past. A crack in the sidewalk where a dandelion has taken root. The smell of rain on hot asphalt. The way a shadow stretches and shrinks as you pass under a streetlight. The sound of a distant train whistle, lonesome and familiar. These are the moments that make up a life, and they are almost always available to us, free of charge, if we are willing to slow down enough to notice them.

There is a word in German, *Waldeinsamkeit*, that translates roughly to “the feeling of being alone in the woods,” and it captures something that I think many of us long for without knowing how to name it. It is not loneliness, exactly, and it is not solitude in the sense of being isolated from others. It is a kind of companionable aloneness, a sense that you are part of a larger world, a world that does not care about your deadlines or your bank account or your social media presence, a world that is older and slower and more patient than the human world you have built around yourself. The woods do not know your name. The river does not care what you do for a living. And there is a strange relief in that, a relief that I can only describe as a kind of homecoming, as if the deepest part of you recognizes that you were always meant to be part of this larger, slower story, the story of seasons and tides and the slow growth of trees.

I have been thinking a lot about time lately, about how we experience it and how we measure it and how we try to control it. We have invented clocks and calendars and schedules, and we have convinced ourselves that time is something we can manage, something we can save or spend or waste. But the time that matters most is not the time on the clock. It is the time that passes without our noticing it, the time that folds in on itself when we are reading a good book or walking through the woods or sitting with someone we love. The philosopher Henri Bergson called this *durée*, or duration, and he distinguished it from the abstract, mathematical time of clocks. Duration is the time we actually live, the time that flows through us like water through a stream. It cannot be measured or divided into equal parts. It stretches and compresses depending on what we are doing and how we are feeling. An hour spent in the dentist’s chair can feel like a week. An hour spent watching the sunset can feel like a minute. And yet both are the same sixty minutes by the clock. What changes is our experience of them, our sense of being inside time rather than outside it.

I think walking is a way of experiencing duration, of reconnecting with the slow, textured time of the body. When you walk without a destination, you are not trying to get anywhere. You are not watching the clock. You are simply moving through space, and in that movement, time seems to open up, to become wider and deeper. A twenty-minute walk can feel like an hour. A two-hour walk can feel like a day. And the strange thing is that when you return home, you feel as if you have been away much longer than you actually have, as if the walk has taken you somewhere that cannot be measured in miles or minutes, somewhere inside yourself that you had forgotten was there.

I have also been thinking about memory, and how walking can be a way of remembering, not just in the sense of recalling the past, but in the sense of re-membering, of putting the pieces of ourselves back together. There is something about moving through a familiar place that brings back not just the big events of our lives, but the small, sensory details that we thought we had lost. A particular smell—the damp earthiness of a basement, the sweet mustiness of old books, the sharp tang of cut grass—can send us hurtling back to a moment we had not thought about in decades. A certain angle of light through a window can suddenly evoke a room we once knew, a person we once loved, a feeling we thought we had outgrown. The body remembers what the mind forgets, and walking is one of the ways we can access that bodily memory, that deep archive of sensation and emotion that lives beneath the level of conscious thought.

I remember a winter evening, years ago, when I was walking home from a friend’s apartment through a neighborhood I did not know well. It had snowed earlier in the day, and the snow had frozen into a thin crust that crunched under my boots. The streetlights cast pools of orange light on the white ground, and the air was so cold that it felt sharp in my lungs, almost metallic. I was not thinking about anything in particular. I was just walking, enjoying the emptiness of the streets, the sense of being the only person awake in a sleeping city. And then, suddenly, I was overcome by a feeling of intense, almost unbearable happiness. It came from nowhere, or rather it came from everywhere—from the texture of the snow, from the silence, from the rhythm of my own steps, from the sheer fact of being alive in that moment, in that body, in that winter night. I have never been able to explain that feeling, and I have never been able to reproduce it. But I have never forgotten it. It remains in my memory as a kind of proof that the world is more than it appears to be, that there are moments of grace hidden in the ordinary, if only we are willing to walk out into them.

There is a tradition in literature of the walker as philosopher, as observer, as seeker. The French poet Charles Baudelaire wrote about the *flâneur*, the stroller who wanders through the city not to buy anything or meet anyone, but simply to watch, to absorb, to become one with the crowd. The American writer Henry David Thoreau walked for hours every day in the woods around Walden Pond, and he wrote that he could not preserve his health or spirits unless he spent at least four hours a day “sauntering through the woods and over the hills and fields, absolutely free from all worldly engagements.” The word “sauntering,” Thoreau noted, might come from the French *sainte-terre*, meaning “holy land,” or from *sans terre*, meaning “without land,” without a fixed home, without a destination. To saunter, in this sense, is to walk as a pilgrim, to walk as if you are always on your way to a holy place, even when you have no idea where that place is.

I like that idea. I like the thought that walking can be a kind of pilgrimage, not because it leads to a sacred site, but because it leads us back to ourselves, to the ground beneath our feet, to the present moment that is always available to us if we will only show up for it. The sacred is not somewhere else. It is here, in the cracked sidewalk, in the gray sky, in the sound of the wind in the wires. It is in the ordinary, the overlooked, the taken-for-granted. And walking is one of the ways we can learn to see it.

I want to write about the body, too, about how walking reminds us that we are not just minds floating in a void, but embodied creatures, made of bone and muscle and blood, subject to gravity and weather and fatigue. We spend so much of our lives sitting, hunched over screens, our bodies forgotten, our posture crumbling, our eyes straining. And then we wonder why we feel so disconnected, so anxious, so unreal. The body is not a burden we have to carry. It is the only way we have of being in the world, the only way we have of touching, tasting, smelling, hearing, seeing. And walking is the simplest way to honor it, to give it what it needs, to remind ourselves that we are alive in the most literal, physical sense. When you walk, you can feel your heart beating, your lungs expanding, your legs moving in their ancient, steady rhythm. You are not thinking about your body. You are your body, and your body is you, and for a little while, at least, there is no gap between the mind and the flesh, no division between the thinker and the thought.

Sometimes I think that the greatest gift of walking is that it teaches us how to be bored. We live in an age that is terrified of boredom, an age that has invented a thousand devices to prevent it, an age that treats every empty moment as a problem to be solved, a void to be filled. But boredom is not the enemy. It is a doorway. When we are bored, when we have nothing to do, when we are just walking down a street with no phone in our hand and no music in our ears, the mind begins to wander. It drifts. It makes connections it would never make if it were busy and distracted. It remembers things it had forgotten. It imagines things it had never imagined. Boredom is the soil in which creativity grows, and walking is one of the most reliable ways to cultivate it. I have had some of my best ideas while walking, not because I was trying to have ideas, but because I had given myself permission to be aimless, to be empty, to let the mind do whatever it wanted to do. And what it wanted to do, it turns out, was to play, to dream, to see the world with new eyes.

There is also something political about walking, I think. Walking is one of the most democratic of activities. It requires no special equipment, no membership, no training. Anyone can do it, rich or poor, young or old, regardless of their background or beliefs. The sidewalk is public space, the trail is open to all, and when we walk, we are participating in an ancient human practice that goes back to the very beginning of our species. We are bipedal animals. We evolved to walk. Our entire bodies are shaped by the act of walking, from the arches of our feet to the curve of our spines. And yet we have built a world that is hostile to walking, a world of sprawling suburbs and stroads and parking lots, a world where the pedestrian is an afterthought, a nuisance, a target. To walk in such a world is to make a kind of statement, to assert that we are not just consumers, not just cogs in a machine, but human beings with bodies and desires and a right to occupy the earth at our own pace.

I think about the great walkers of history, the ones who turned walking into an art or a philosophy or a political act. I think about Gandhi, who walked 240 miles to the sea to make salt, a walk that became a symbol of resistance to empire. I think about the Civil Rights marchers who walked from Selma to Montgomery, their feet carrying them through tear gas and batons and the murderous hatred of their fellow citizens, their steps a testament to the power of nonviolent struggle. I think about the pilgrims who have walked the Camino de Santiago for over a thousand years, and the poets who have walked the streets of their cities looking for lines, for images, for the exact word that would capture the ache of being alive. Walking is never just walking. It is always also a way of saying something, of being something, of becoming something.

I have been sitting at this desk for a long time now, and the light has changed. The maple tree outside the window is no longer lit from above but from the side, and the leaves have taken on a deep, almost fiery orange. The sky has gone from blue to a pale, watery gray, and there is a hint of rain in the air, that particular smell that comes before a storm, a smell like wet dust and ozone and something else, something green and growing. I should go for a walk. I should close this document and put on my shoes and step outside. I have written about walking long enough; it is time to do it. But before I go, I want to say one more thing, a thing that feels important, a thing that I am only now beginning to understand as I write these words.

Writing freely, like walking freely, is not about the destination. It is not even about the process, exactly, about the getting somewhere or the doing of the thing. It is about opening yourself to the unknown, about trusting that the path will appear beneath your feet, about being willing to be surprised by where you end up. When I started this essay, I had no idea what I was going to write. I had only a desk, a window, a maple tree, and a vague sense that I wanted to say something true about something that mattered. And now, a few thousand words later, I find that I have written about walking, about memory, about time, about the body, about boredom, about politics, about the sacred. I did not plan any of this. It emerged, the way a path emerges when you are walking through a forest, one step at a time. And that is the miracle of freedom, both in writing and in walking: it does not give you the answers. It gives you the space to find them.

So I am going to close this document now. I am going to stand up, and walk away from the desk, and go outside into the fading light. I am going to walk without a destination, without a plan, without anything in my pockets but my keys and my hands. I am going to let the streets take me wherever they want to go. And if I am lucky, if I am open, if I am willing to be bored and surprised and present, I may find something I did not know I was looking for. Or I may find nothing at all, which would also be fine. Because walking, like writing, is not about finding. It is about seeking. And seeking, I have learned, is its own reward.

It gives you the space to find them.

So I am going to close this document now. I am going to stand up, and walk away from the desk, and go outside into the fading light. I am going to walk without a destination, without a plan, without anything in my pockets but my keys and my hands. I am going to let the streets take me wherever they want to go. And if I am lucky, if I am open, if I am willing to be bored and surprised and present, I may find something I did not know I was looking for. Or I may find nothing at all, which would also be fine. Because walking, like writing, is not about finding. It is about seeking. And seeking, I have learned, is its own reward.
